title: Ai Taken and the Covenant Renewed at Mount Ebal
summary: The LORD encourages Joshua and gives him a plan for Ai. Part of the army lies in ambush west of the city while Joshua draws Ai's defenders out with a feigned retreat; at the signal of Joshua's outstretched lance, the ambush seizes and burns the city, and the defenders are trapped and destroyed. Israel may keep the livestock and plunder this time. Joshua then builds an altar on Mount Ebal, writes a copy of the law on stones, and reads all the law, with its blessings and curses, to the whole assembly of Israel, including women, children, and foreigners.
story: Chapter 7 ended with Achan's judgment and the LORD's anger turning away. Now the story resumes where it broke off. God speaks the same words of encouragement he spoke in Joshua 1 (Do not be afraid or discouraged) and gives Joshua a plan, and the town that humiliated Israel falls. The first half of the chapter shows Israel restored to God's favor. The second half turns from war to worship: before going any further, Israel fulfills Moses' command in Deuteronomy 11:29 and 27:1-8 to write the law on stones and proclaim blessings and curses from Mounts Gerizim and Ebal. With this act, the first stage of the entry into the land ends where it should, with Israel bound again to the covenant. Chapter 9 will turn to the kings of the land and the Gibeonites.
historical:
Ai lay east of Bethel in the central hill country, and the ambush is set between the two (verses 9, 12). The note that the men of Bethel also went out after Israel (verse 17) suggests that the two towns acted together. On the archaeological difficulties surrounding Ai's location, see the note on chapter 7.

Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim stand on either side of the valley where the ancient city of Shechem lay, near modern Nablus, about twenty miles north of Ai. Shechem was an important Canaanite city and a place where Abraham built an altar (Genesis 12:6-7) and Jacob bought land (Genesis 33:18-20). In the 1980s the Israeli archaeologist Adam Zertal excavated a stone structure on Mount Ebal that he identified as an early Israelite altar, possibly connected with this account. Others have interpreted the structure as a farmhouse or watchtower, and its significance continues to be debated.
cultural:
Ambush and feigned retreat were standard tactics in ancient warfare; the same strategy appears in Judges 20:29-48 against Gibeah. Joshua's outstretched lance (verses 18, 26) served as a signal to the hidden troops, but it also recalls Moses holding up his hands with the staff of God during the battle against Amalek (Exodus 17:8-13). The permission to take livestock and plunder (verses 2, 27) shows that not every city was placed under the full ban; Deuteronomy 20:14 allowed plunder in some cases. The contrast with Achan is pointed: had he waited, the goods of the next city would have been his by permission.

The treatment of the king of Ai's body (verse 29) follows Deuteronomy 21:22-23: a body hung on a tree after execution had to be taken down by evening, because one hanged on a tree was under God's curse and the land must not be defiled. The altar of uncut stones follows Exodus 20:25, which forbade dressing altar stones with iron tools. Writing the law on stones coated with plaster, as Deuteronomy 27:2-4 commands, was a known method of public inscription. The reading of the whole law to men, women, children, and foreigners (verse 35) matches Deuteronomy 31:12, making the covenant the possession of every person in the community, not only the leaders.

The report that twelve thousand men and women of Ai fell (verse 25) raises the same moral question as Jericho. Christians have answered it in several ways, set out more fully in the note on chapter 6: as God's judgment on Canaan's long sin (Genesis 15:16), limited to that moment and never a pattern for later war; as the stock, sweeping language of ancient war reports, which the book itself qualifies when it admits that many Canaanites remained; as a stage in Israel's understanding to be read in the light of Christ; and, since Origen, as a figure of the believer's war against sin. Many readers hold more than one of these together.
literary: The chapter has two very different halves. The battle account (verses 1-29) is detailed and suspenseful, full of movement words (ambush, flee, pursue, turn, strike) and careful notes of position (behind, west, north, between). It deliberately reverses chapter 7: Israel again appears to flee from Ai, but this time the flight is a trap. The motif of the outstretched lance frames the victory (verses 18, 26). The account ends with a heap of stones over the king of Ai (verse 29), echoing the heap over Achan in 7:26. The covenant ceremony (verses 30-35) is written in a calm, formal style and repeats the phrase as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded, showing Joshua's complete obedience. The final verse stresses that there was not a word of all that Moses had commanded that Joshua failed to read, the opposite of Achan's partial obedience.

outline.t: The LORD encourages Joshua and gives the plan
The feigned retreat draws out Ai's army
The lance raised and the city taken
Ai destroyed and its king executed
The altar, the law, and the covenant at Mount Ebal

doctrines.note: Once the sin in the camp has been dealt with, God speaks words of encouragement again and gives victory. Restoration follows the removal of sin.
Before going further, Israel renews the covenant at Ebal and Gerizim, hearing the blessings and curses of the law. The land is held on covenant terms.
Joshua writes the law on stones and reads every word to the whole people, including children and foreigners. God's word is public, complete, and meant for everyone.
Worship follows victory: burnt offerings and peace offerings on an altar built as God commanded. Israel's first act of settled worship in the land is thanksgiving and communion with God.

words.note: Arav, to lie in wait or ambush. The word appears repeatedly in the battle account. God himself directs the ambush (verse 2), showing that the LORD's war did not always involve miracles; here it involves ordinary strategy, obediently followed.

Kidon, a javelin, lance, or curved sword. Joshua holds it out as a signal and does not lower it until the battle is complete (verse 26). The gesture echoes Moses' raised hands in Exodus 17 and marks the victory as the LORD's.

Mizbeach, altar, from the verb to slaughter. The altar on Mount Ebal is built of uncut stones as the law required, and burnt offerings and peace offerings are made there. It marks the first formal worship in the land after the crossing.

Qahal, assembly or congregation. The law is read before the whole assembly of Israel (verse 35), which includes women, little ones, and foreigners. The Greek translation often rendered qahal with ekklesia, the word the New Testament uses for the church.

christ: The body of the king of Ai hung on a tree and taken down at sunset (verse 29) follows the law of Deuteronomy 21:23, which says that anyone hung on a tree is under God's curse. Paul quotes that law in Galatians 3:13: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. For it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree.’” The Gospels also note that Jesus' body was taken down from the cross before evening (John 19:31). What was a sign of defeat and curse for Israel's enemy becomes, in the New Testament, the place where Christ bore the curse for others. The reading of the blessings and curses at Ebal also sets the covenant terms that the rest of the Old Testament traces: Israel's failure brings the curses, and the prophets look for a new covenant. The New Testament presents Christ as the one through whom the blessing of Abraham comes to the nations (Galatians 3:14). These connections come from the later story, not from hidden meanings in Joshua 8.

hard.q: Why does the covenant ceremony at Mount Ebal appear here, when Ebal lies far north of Ai and Israel had not yet conquered that region?
hard.a: The placement of verses 30-35 is a genuine puzzle. Mount Ebal is about twenty miles north of Ai, in territory the book has not yet described Israel taking, and Joshua 9:1 continues as though no such trip had happened. Ancient manuscripts differ: the Greek Septuagint places this passage after 9:2, and one Dead Sea Scrolls manuscript of Joshua appears to place a similar account right after the Jordan crossing. Interpreters respond in several ways. Some think Israel marched to Shechem without opposition, perhaps because the region was friendly or thinly populated, and note that the Bible does not record a conquest of Shechem at all. Others think the passage has been placed here for theological rather than chronological reasons, to show that Israel's first priority after restoring its obedience was covenant renewal, as Moses had commanded for the day they crossed the Jordan (Deuteronomy 27:2). Critical scholars often regard the variation among manuscripts as evidence that the passage was inserted at different points by later editors. The text's message is the same on each view: the land is received under the word of God.

questions: The same town that defeated Israel falls once the sin is dealt with. Where has unresolved sin kept you from moving forward?
Joshua read every word of the law to everyone, including children and foreigners. Who in your community might be left out of hearing God's word, and how could that change?
Israel stopped between battles to worship and renew the covenant. How do you make room for worship in the middle of pressure and busy seasons?
